title: Nvidia CEO to G20: Don’t Regulate the Robot Apocalypse Just Yet
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

#Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has urged G20 governments to regulate artificial intelligence according to demonstrated problems rather than “theoretical harms.” Speaking alongside US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at a meeting in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, Huang aligned himself with the Trump administration’s campaign for lighter regulation.

The debate extends beyond safety rules to copyrighted material used to train AI systems. #Lutnick called on #G20 countries to embrace “fair use,” allowing developers to train models on creators’ work while protecting artists and inventors. He offered no mechanism for striking that balance. Authors, publishers and media groups have sued #Anthropic, #OpenAI, #Google and #Meta, alleging that their work was used without authorization.

The US Justice Department reinforced the administration’s position by supporting OpenAI in its copyright dispute with The New York Times. It argued that training AI models qualifies as fair use. Technology companies say large datasets are essential for innovation; creators counter that their rights and livelihoods require safeguards and compensation.

Huang’s intervention captures the central tension facing policymakers: acting too early or broadly could delay new models, change how products operate and weaken growth, while waiting for proven damage could leave governments reacting only after harm occurs. Other figures offered different emphases at the G20 gathering. Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis advocated safety testing, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg opposed restrictions on open-weight models, and Elon Musk criticized European Union technology rules. The contest is therefore not simply regulation versus innovation, but which risks merit action, when, and who bears the cost.

Source: Reuters
